claims.evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experiments showing no fast glutamatergic responses in POMC, NPY/AgRP, and Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons from KO animals (Figure 12).

claims.claim: Deleting Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons led to conditioned place preference for sucrose in E2-treated KO female mice.
claims.source: Deleting Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons eliminated glutamate release and led to conditioned place preference for sucrose in E2-treated KO female mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiments showing that E2-treated KO mice developed a preference for the sucrose-paired chamber (Figure 16A).

claims.claim: The E2-driven increase in Kiss1 neuronal excitability and glutamate neurotransmission may play a key role in governing the motivational drive for palatable food in females.
claims.source: Therefore, the E2-driven increase in Kiss1 neuronal excitability and glutamate neurotransmission may play a key role in governing the motivational drive for palatable food in females.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the integration of electrophysiological and behavioral findings.

claims.claim: Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons are essential for positive feedback by estradiol on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neuronal activity and the luteinizing hormone (LH) surge in rodents.
claims.source: Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons are essential for positive feedback by estradiol on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neuronal activity and the luteinizing hormone (LH) surge in rodents (Clarkson et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clarkson et al., 2008.

claims.claim: 17β-estradiol (E2) increases Kiss1 mRNA expression in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
claims.source: 17β-estradiol (E2) increases Kiss1 mRNA expression in these rostral Kiss1 neurons (Smith et al., 2005), and their excitability is increased by the E2-driven upregulation of T-type calcium, hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic-nucleotide gated (h)- and persistent sodium (INaP) currents (Piet et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015,2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The excitability of Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons is increased by the E2-driven upregulation of T-type calcium, hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic-nucleotide gated (h)- and persistent sodium (INaP) currents.
claims.source: 17β-estradiol (E2) increases Kiss1 mRNA expression in these rostral Kiss1 neurons (Smith et al., 2005), and their excitability is increased by the E2-driven upregulation of T-type calcium, hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic-nucleotide gated (h)- and persistent sodium (INaP) currents (Piet et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015,2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Piet et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015, 2013.

claims.claim: Glutamate induces burst firing and pacemaking activity in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
claims.source: In addition, glutamate induces burst firing and pacemaking activity in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Wang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013.

claims.claim: E2 significantly inhibits Kiss1 mRNA expression in ARH neurons.
claims.source: In contrast to the Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, E2 significantly inhibits Kiss1 mRNA expression in ARH neurons (Lehman et al., 2010; Navarro et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lehman et al., 2010; Navarro et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Kiss1ARH neurons co-express the peptide neurotransmitters kisspeptin (Kiss1), tachykinin 2 (Tac2; a.k.a. neurokinin B; NKB) and dynorphin.
claims.source: Kiss1ARH neurons co-express the peptide neurotransmitters kisspeptin (Kiss1), tachykinin 2 (Tac2; a.k.a. neurokinin B; NKB) and dynorphin (Lehman et al., 2013), which have been proposed to be responsible for pulsatile release of GnRH and LH (Clarkson et al., 2017; Li et al., 2009; Navarro et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lehman et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Kisspeptin, Tac2, and dynorphin have been proposed to be responsible for pulsatile release of GnRH and LH.
claims.source: Kiss1ARH neurons co-express the peptide neurotransmitters kisspeptin (Kiss1), tachykinin 2 (Tac2; a.k.a. neurokinin B; NKB) and dynorphin (Lehman et al., 2013), which have been proposed to be responsible for pulsatile release of GnRH and LH (Clarkson et al., 2017; Li et al., 2009; Navarro et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clarkson et al., 2017; Li et al., 2009; Navarro et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The cellular mechanisms by which Kiss1ARH neurons synchronize to drive GnRH pulses involves a combination of co-released Tac2 excitation via Tac3 receptors and dynorphin presynaptic inhibition via κ-opioid receptors.
claims.source: Indeed, the cellular mechanisms by which Kiss1ARH neurons synchronize to drive GnRH pulses was recently elucidated and involves a combination of co-released Tac2 excitation via Tac3 receptors and dynorphin presynaptic inhibition via κ-opioid receptors (Qiu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Qiu et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Kiss1ARH neurons express the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (vGluT2).
claims.source: Kiss1ARH neurons also express the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (vGluT2) (Cravo et al., 2011; Nestor et al., 2016), an indication that they have the potential to package and release the neurotransmitter glutamate (Herman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cravo et al., 2011; Nestor et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Expression of vGluT2 indicates that Kiss1ARH neurons have the potential to package and release the neurotransmitter glutamate.
claims.source: Kiss1ARH neurons also express the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (vGluT2) (Cravo et al., 2011; Nestor et al., 2016), an indication that they have the potential to package and release the neurotransmitter glutamate (Herman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Herman et al., 2014 and is based on established knowledge about vGluT2 function.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Kiss1ARH neurons evokes glutamatergic EPSCs in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
claims.source: Optogenetic activation of Kiss1ARH neurons evokes glutamatergic EPSCs not only in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Qiu et al., 2016) but also in proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and neuropeptide Y/agouti-related peptide (NPY/AgRP) neurons (Nestor et al., 2016), which further establishes direct functional connections between Kiss1ARH neurons and hypothalamic neurons important for the control of reproduction and energy homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Qiu et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Kiss1ARH neurons evokes glutamatergic EPSCs in proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and neuropeptide Y/agouti-related peptide (NPY/AgRP) neurons.
claims.source: Optogenetic activation of Kiss1ARH neurons evokes glutamatergic EPSCs not only in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Qiu et al., 2016) but also in proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and neuropeptide Y/agouti-related peptide (NPY/AgRP) neurons (Nestor et al., 2016), which further establishes direct functional connections between Kiss1ARH neurons and hypothalamic neurons important for the control of reproduction and energy homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nestor et al., 2016.

claims.claim: In males, Slc17a6 mRNA and glutamate release are increased in gonadectomized as compared to intact animals.
claims.source: In males, Slc17a6 (encodes vGluT2) mRNA and glutamate release are increased in gonadectomized as compared to intact animals, an indication of inhibitory effects of gonadal steroids on glutamate neurotransmission in these neurons (Nestor et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nestor et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Gonadal steroids have inhibitory effects on glutamate neurotransmission in Kiss1ARH neurons in males.
claims.source: In males, Slc17a6 (encodes vGluT2) mRNA and glutamate release are increased in gonadectomized as compared to intact animals, an indication of inhibitory effects of gonadal steroids on glutamate neurotransmission in these neurons (Nestor et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that gonadectomy increases Slc17a6 mRNA and glutamate release.

claims.claim: There are pronounced male/female differences in feeding behavior.
claims.source: Based on pronounced male/female differences in feeding behavior and the excitatory glutamatergic input from Kiss1ARH neurons to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons in females (Asarian and Geary, 2006; Qiu et al., 2016), we hypothesized that the mRNA expression of Slc17a6 and glutamate release in females in contrast to males, would be amplified by E2 in Kiss1ARH neurons in order to help maintain reproduction during different energy states.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Asarian and Geary, 2006.

claims.claim: Tac2 mRNA was the most highly expressed in Kiss1ARH neurons from OVX females.
claims.source: Based on the CT values (Figure 1) and quantitative analysis with Tacr3 as calibrator (see Materials and Methods), Tac2 mRNA was the most highly expressed in Kiss1ARH neurons from OVX females, such that Tac2 >>> (50-fold) Pdyn ≥Kiss1 >> (6-fold) Slc17a6, and with E2 treatment, Tac2 >> (18-fold) Pdyn >> (2-fold) Slc17a6 > (2-fold) Kiss1 (one-way ANOVA).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1 and quantitative analysis.

claims.claim: In OVX females, Tac2 mRNA expression is 50-fold higher than Pdyn and Kiss1, and 6-fold higher than Slc17a6 in Kiss1ARH neurons.
claims.source: Based on the CT values (Figure 1) and quantitative analysis with Tacr3 as calibrator (see Materials and Methods), Tac2 mRNA was the most highly expressed in Kiss1ARH neurons from OVX females, such that Tac2 >>> (50-fold) Pdyn ≥Kiss1 >> (6-fold) Slc17a6, and with E2 treatment, Tac2 >> (18-fold) Pdyn >> (2-fold) Slc17a6 > (2-fold) Kiss1 (one-way ANOVA).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of qPCR data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: With E2 treatment, Tac2 mRNA expression is 18-fold higher than Pdyn, 2-fold higher than Slc17a6, and 2-fold higher than Kiss1 in Kiss1ARH neurons.
claims.source: Based on the CT values (Figure 1) and quantitative analysis with Tacr3 as calibrator (see Materials and Methods), Tac2 mRNA was the most highly expressed in Kiss1ARH neurons from OVX females, such that Tac2 >>> (50-fold) Pdyn ≥Kiss1 >> (6-fold) Slc17a6, and with E2 treatment, Tac2 >> (18-fold) Pdyn >> (2-fold) Slc17a6 > (2-fold) Kiss1 (one-way ANOVA).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of qPCR data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: E2 increased the mRNA expression of Cacna1g in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that the mRNA expression of Cacna1g and Hcn1 and Hcn2 were significantly increased in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: E2 increased the mRNA expression of Hcn1 in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that the mRNA expression of Cacna1g and Hcn1 and Hcn2 were significantly increased in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: E2 increased the mRNA expression of Hcn2 in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that the mRNA expression of Cacna1g and Hcn1 and Hcn2 were significantly increased in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated females as compared to oil-treated, OVX females (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Kiss1 mRNA levels were significantly reduced by E2 in Kiss1ARH neurons.
claims.source: For comparison we also measured Kiss1 and Pdyn mRNAs in the same neuronal pools, and as predicted, Kiss1 and Pdyn mRNA levels were significantly reduced by E2 (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Pdyn mRNA levels were significantly reduced by E2 in Kiss1ARH neurons.
claims.source: For comparison we also measured Kiss1 and Pdyn mRNAs in the same neuronal pools, and as predicted, Kiss1 and Pdyn mRNA levels were significantly reduced by E2 (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Both T- and h-currents were increased in Kiss1ARH neurons with E2-treatment as compared to oil-treatment.
claims.source: In addition, both T- and h-currents (Figure 2B) as well as neuronal excitability (measured as rebound excitation; Figure 2C) were increased in Kiss1ARH neurons with E2-treatment as compared to oil-treatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Neuronal excitability (measured as rebound excitation) was increased in Kiss1ARH neurons with E2-treatment as compared to oil-treatment.
claims.source: In addition, both T- and h-currents (Figure 2B) as well as neuronal excitability (measured as rebound excitation; Figure 2C) were increased in Kiss1ARH neurons with E2-treatment as compared to oil-treatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Although E2-treatment downregulates neuropeptide expression in Kiss1ARH neurons, it significantly increases the intrinsic conductances and hence the excitability of these vital neurons.
claims.source: Therefore, although E2-treatment downregulates neuropeptide expression in Kiss1ARH neurons, it significantly increases the intrinsic conductances and hence the excitability of these vital neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Kiss1ARH neurons in E2-treated, OVX female mice expressed approximately 2-fold higher levels of Slc17a6 mRNA than oil-treated, OVX mice.
claims.source: The qPCR analysis revealed that Kiss1ARH neurons (5 cells/pool; 3–6 pools/animal) in E2-treated, OVX female mice expressed approximately 2-fold higher levels of Slc17a6 mRNA than oil-treated, OVX mice (Figure 3), while the level of Slc32a1 mRNA was undetectable in Kiss1ARH neurons from both groups of female mice (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The level of Slc32a1 mRNA was undetectable in Kiss1ARH neurons from both oil-treated and E2-treated OVX female mice.
claims.source: The qPCR analysis revealed that Kiss1ARH neurons (5 cells/pool; 3–6 pools/animal) in E2-treated, OVX female mice expressed approximately 2-fold higher levels of Slc17a6 mRNA than oil-treated, OVX mice (Figure 3), while the level of Slc32a1 mRNA was undetectable in Kiss1ARH neurons from both groups of female mice (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on qPCR data that showed Slc32a1 mRNA was below the level of detectability.

claims.claim: The mRNA expression of Tac2 was significantly reduced in E2-treated females compared to oil-treated females.
claims.source: For comparison we also measured Tac2 and Tacr3 mRNAs in the same Kiss1ARH neuronal pools, and as expected, the mRNA expression of these transcripts were both significantly reduced in E2-treated females (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The mRNA expression of Tacr3 was significantly reduced in E2-treated females compared to oil-treated females.
claims.source: For comparison we also measured Tac2 and Tacr3 mRNAs in the same Kiss1ARH neuronal pools, and as expected, the mRNA expression of these transcripts were both significantly reduced in E2-treated females (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The E2-induced increased Slc17a6 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons is an indication that the amino acid neurotransmitter glutamate is regulated differently by E2 than the neuropeptides in females.
claims.source: Therefore, the E2-induced increased Slc17a6 mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons is an indication that the amino acid neurotransmitter glutamate is regulated differently by E2 than the neuropeptides in females.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential regulation of Slc17a6 (increased) versus neuropeptides (decreased) by E2.

claims.claim: Seventy-seven cells showed an inward current following photostimulation with a mean amplitude of 29.8 ± 3.4 pA, a mean latency to peak of 4.0 ± 0.1 ms, and an average decay time constant of 5.5 ± 0.6 ms.
claims.source: In total, seventy-seven cells showed an inward current following photostimulation with a mean amplitude of 29.8 ± 3.4 pA, a mean latency to peak of 4.0 ± 0.1 ms, and an average decay time constant of 5.5 ± 0.6 ms.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiological measurements from optogenetic experiments.

claims.claim: The light-induced response in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons was blocked with the AMPA- and NMDA-receptor blockers, CNQX and AP5, respectively.
claims.source: This light-induced response was blocked with the AMPA- and NMDA-receptor blockers, CNQX and AP5, respectively (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Glutamate, and not GABA, is the primary amino acid neurotransmitter released from Kiss1ARH neurons in females.
claims.source: Therefore, glutamate, and not GABA, is the primary amino acid neurotransmitter released from Kiss1ARH neurons in females.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that the light-induced response was blocked by glutamate receptor antagonists.

claims.claim: TTX abrogated the photostimulated post-synaptic inward current in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons, but the light-induced response could be rescued with the addition of the potassium channel blocker 4-AP.
claims.source: Moreover, although TTX (1 μM) abrogated the photostimulated post-synaptic inward current, we could rescue the light-induced response with the addition of the potassium channel blocker 4-AP (100 μM to the bath) in both POMC (n = 3) and NPY/AgRP (n = 2) neurons (Figure 4D,E), which is biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling from Kiss1ARH neurons to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons (Cousin and Robinson, 2000; Petreanu et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claims.claim: The rescue of the light-induced response with 4-AP is biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling from Kiss1ARH neurons to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons.
claims.source: Moreover, although TTX (1 μM) abrogated the photostimulated post-synaptic inward current, we could rescue the light-induced response with the addition of the potassium channel blocker 4-AP (100 μM to the bath) in both POMC (n = 3) and NPY/AgRP (n = 2) neurons (Figure 4D,E), which is biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling from Kiss1ARH neurons to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons (Cousin and Robinson, 2000; Petreanu et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiological data supported by citations to Cousin and Robinson, 2000; Petreanu et al., 2009.

claims.claim: There was no difference in the amplitude of the evoked fast PSCs between POMC and NPY neurons.
claims.source: Based on this analysis, there was no difference in the amplitude of the evoked fast PSCs between POMC and NPY neurons (post-hoc identified) (25.8 ± 4.8 pA, n = 36 POMC neurons versus 33.3 ± 4.9 pA, n = 41 NPY/AgRP neurons).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiological measurements comparing POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons.

claims.claim: When Kiss1ARH neurons in the female are firing at low frequencies there is equivalent fast (ionotropic) glutamatergic input to both POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons in the female, similar to what we found in males.
claims.source: Therefore, it appears that when Kiss1ARH neurons in the female are firing at low frequencies there is equivalent fast (ionotropic) glutamatergic input to both POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons in the female, similar to what we found in males (Nestor et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological data and comparison to previous findings in males.

claims.claim: POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons in E2-treated, OVX female mice had a significantly lower PPR compared to oil-treated, OVX females.
claims.source: Using a photostimulation PPR protocol of two 5 ms LED stimulations separated by 50 ms (Figure 5A,B), we found that POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons in E2-treated, OVX female mice had a significantly lower PPR compared to oil-treated, OVX females in both POMC neurons (Figure 5C,D) and in NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 5E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio experiments shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: A lower PPR indicates that there is a greater probability of glutamate release with the first stimulus in E2-treated, OVX animals.
claims.source: These results indicate that there is a greater probability of glutamate release with the first stimulus in E2-treated, OVX animals (Figure 5B), which is consistent with higher mRNA expression of Slc17a6 in Kiss1ARH neurons following E2-treatment.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the paired-pulse ratio data based on established principles of synaptic physiology.

claims.claim: The lower PPR in E2-treated animals is consistent with higher mRNA expression of Slc17a6 in Kiss1ARH neurons following E2-treatment.
claims.source: These results indicate that there is a greater probability of glutamate release with the first stimulus in E2-treated, OVX animals (Figure 5B), which is consistent with higher mRNA expression of Slc17a6 in Kiss1ARH neurons following E2-treatment.
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the electrophysiological findings to the molecular data.

claims.claim: There is a striking male/female difference concerning the effects of sex steroids (testosterone versus estradiol) on Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamate release in Kiss1ARH neurons.
claims.source: Collectively, these data indicate that there is a striking male/female difference concerning the effects of sex steroids (testosterone versus estradiol) on Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamate release in Kiss1ARH neurons (Nestor et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current findings in females and previous findings in males cited from Nestor et al., 2016.

claims.claim: ChR2-mCherry injections labeled Kiss1ARH neurons within the arcuate nucleus only.
claims.source: Currently we confirmed that ChR2-mCherry injections labeled Kiss1ARH neurons within the arcuate nucleus only (Figure 6A1), and sent extensive fiber-projections rostrally to the AVPV/PeN area in the vicinity of immunoreactive Kiss1 neurons (Figure 6A2,A3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6A1.

claims.claim: ChR2-mCherry labeled Kiss1ARH neurons sent extensive fiber-projections rostrally to the AVPV/PeN area in the vicinity of immunoreactive Kiss1 neurons.
claims.source: Currently we confirmed that ChR2-mCherry injections labeled Kiss1ARH neurons within the arcuate nucleus only (Figure 6A1), and sent extensive fiber-projections rostrally to the AVPV/PeN area in the vicinity of immunoreactive Kiss1 neurons (Figure 6A2,A3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6A2,A3.

claims.claim: ChR2-mCherry expressing cell bodies were not found in the AVPV/PeN.
claims.source: Notably, ChR2-mCherry expressing cell bodies were not found in the AVPV/PeN.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the immunocytochemistry experiments.

claims.claim: Photostimulation-induced an inward current in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, which was blocked in the presence of TTX but rescued with addition of 4-AP in the presence of TTX.
claims.source: Photostimulation-induced an inward current in Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, which was blocked in the presence of TTX (1 μM) but rescued with addition of 4-AP in the presence of TTX (n = 4) (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The rescue of the photostimulation-induced inward current with 4-AP is biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling from Kiss1ARH neurons to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
claims.source: Therefore, this is biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling from Kiss1ARH neurons to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiological data based on established principles.

claims.claim: AVPV/PeN neurons from E2-treated females had reduced PPR, an indication that Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons receive an enhanced glutamatergic input from Kiss1ARH neurons in E2-treated females.
claims.source: Using a photoactivation-PPR protocol of two 5 ms LED stimulations as described above, we found that AVPV/PeN neurons, including Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, from E2-treated females had reduced PPR, an indication that Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, similar to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons, receive an enhanced glutamatergic input from Kiss1ARH neurons in E2-treated females (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio experiments shown in Figure 6D,E.

claims.claim: High-frequency (20 Hz) stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons generated a slow EPSC in POMCEGFP neurons.
claims.source: High-frequency (20 Hz) stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons/fibers generated a slow EPSC in POMCEGFP neurons, and in current clamp the stimulation depolarized POMC neurons and increased their firing rate (Figure 7A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: High-frequency stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons depolarized POMC neurons and increased their firing rate.
claims.source: High-frequency (20 Hz) stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons/fibers generated a slow EPSC in POMCEGFP neurons, and in current clamp the stimulation depolarized POMC neurons and increased their firing rate (Figure 7A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: High-frequency optogenetic stimulation generated a slow IPSC in NPYGFP neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, high-frequency optogenetic stimulation generated a slow IPSC in NPYGFP neurons, and in current clamp the same stimulus hyperpolarized and inhibited NPY neurons (Figure 7A,D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: High-frequency stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons hyperpolarized and inhibited NPY neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, high-frequency optogenetic stimulation generated a slow IPSC in NPYGFP neurons, and in current clamp the same stimulus hyperpolarized and inhibited NPY neurons (Figure 7A,D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: The high frequency response in NPY/AgRP neurons was blocked approximately 90% by the mGluR7 antagonist ADX71743.
claims.source: This high frequency response was blocked approximately 90% by the mGluR7 antagonist ADX71743 (IPSP reduced from 5.9 ± 1.2 mV to 0.6 ± 0.2 mV, n = 5; paired t-test, t(4) = 4.281, p=0.013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments with the mGluR7 antagonist.

claims.claim: The change in membrane potential following Kiss1ARH stimulation was significantly different between POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons.
claims.source: The change in membrane potential following Kiss1ARH stimulation was significantly different between POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: High-frequency activity in Kiss1ARH neurons, which through presumably glutamate spillover to extrasynaptic mGluRs, excites POMC but inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons.
claims.source: Therefore, high-frequency activity in Kiss1ARH neurons, which through presumably glutamate spillover to extrasynaptic mGluRs (Nietz et al., 2017; Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003), excites POMC but inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological data and supported by citations to Nietz et al., 2017; Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003.

claims.claim: POMC neurons expressed group I metabotropic glutamate receptor, mGluR1 and/or mGluR5.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that POMC neurons expressed group I metabotropic glutamate receptor, mGluR1 and/or mGluR5 (mGluR1, 44%, n = 5 animals; mGluR5, 21%, n = 5 animals) (Figure 8A,B), whereas NPY/AgRP neurons expressed primarily the group III metabotropic glutamate receptors, mGluR7, with a few neurons also expressing the group II mGluR2 (mGluR7, 50%, n = 5 animals; mGluR2, 13%; n = 4 animals) (Figure 8C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claims.claim: NPY/AgRP neurons expressed primarily the group III metabotropic glutamate receptors, mGluR7, with a few neurons also expressing the group II mGluR2.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that POMC neurons expressed group I metabotropic glutamate receptor, mGluR1 and/or mGluR5 (mGluR1, 44%, n = 5 animals; mGluR5, 21%, n = 5 animals) (Figure 8A,B), whereas NPY/AgRP neurons expressed primarily the group III metabotropic glutamate receptors, mGluR7, with a few neurons also expressing the group II mGluR2 (mGluR7, 50%, n = 5 animals; mGluR2, 13%; n = 4 animals) (Figure 8C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8C,D.

claims.claim: DHPG (50 μM) depolarized and stimulated firing in POMC neurons.
claims.source: Therefore, we used the mGluR 1/5 agonist DHPG (3,5-dihydroxyphenylglycine) to explore its action in POMC neurons, and found that DHPG (50 μM) depolarized and stimulated firing in POMC neurons (Figure 9A), and induced an inward current in synaptically-isolated POMC neurons (Figure 9B).

results.result: E2 treatment increases the expression of T-type calcium channels (Cacna1g) and HCN channels (Hcn1, Hcn2) in Kiss1ARH neurons, leading to increased T-type calcium and h-currents, and enhanced neuronal excitability measured as rebound excitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C30-C32, C35-C37 are well-supported by qPCR data (Figure 2A) showing significant increases in Cacna1g, Hcn1, and Hcn2 mRNA expression, and electrophysiological measurements (Figure 2B,C) demonstrating increased current densities and rebound excitation in E2-treated animals. Statistical significance is reported with appropriate p-values.

results.result: E2 treatment decreases the mRNA expression of neuropeptides Kiss1, Tac2 (NKB), Pdyn (dynorphin), and Tacr3 in Kiss1ARH neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C33, C34, C40, C41 are supported by qPCR data (Figures 2A, 3) showing significant reductions in Kiss1, Tac2, Pdyn, and Tacr3 mRNA levels in E2-treated versus oil-treated OVX females. This is consistent with established knowledge cited from prior literature and confirmed experimentally.

results.result: E2 treatment increases Slc17a6 (vGluT2) mRNA expression approximately 2-fold in Kiss1ARH neurons, indicating differential regulation of glutamate versus neuropeptide neurotransmitters by E2 in females.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C38, C42 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 3) showing approximately 2-fold higher Slc17a6 mRNA levels in E2-treated versus oil-treated OVX females. The inference that glutamate is regulated differently than neuropeptides is reasonable given the opposing directional changes.

results.result: E2 treatment increases glutamatergic synaptic input to POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons from Kiss1ARH neurons, as evidenced by significantly lower paired-pulse ratios indicating greater probability of glutamate release.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C50-C52 are supported by paired-pulse ratio experiments (Figure 5) showing significantly lower PPR in E2-treated versus oil-treated animals in both POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons. The interpretation that lower PPR indicates greater release probability is based on established synaptic physiology principles.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons evokes glutamatergic responses in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons that are blocked by AMPA/NMDA receptor antagonists and rescued by 4-AP after TTX blockade, providing biophysical evidence for direct synaptic signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 are supported by optogenetic electrophysiology data (Figure 4) showing light-evoked inward currents blocked by CNQX/AP5 and rescued by 4-AP in the presence of TTX. The TTX+4-AP rescue is established biophysical evidence for monosynaptic connections, properly cited.

results.result: High-frequency (20 Hz) optogenetic stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons excites POMC neurons via metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR1/5), generating slow EPSCs and depolarization that increases firing rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C60, C61, C67, C69-C72 are supported by optogenetic data (Figure 7) showing slow EPSCs and depolarization in POMC neurons, scRT-PCR data (Figure 8) showing mGluR1/5 expression, and pharmacology (Figure 9) showing DHPG-induced depolarization. The reversal potential at -30 mV is consistent with cationic current activation.

results.result: High-frequency optogenetic stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons via metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR2/7), generating slow IPSCs and hyperpolarization through GIRK channel activation, with enhanced responses in E2-treated animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C62-C64, C68, C74-C77, C79-C81, C83-C84 are supported by optogenetic data (Figure 7) showing slow IPSCs, scRT-PCR (Figure 8) showing mGluR2/7 expression, pharmacology (Figure 10) showing DCG-IV and AMN082-induced hyperpolarization with reversal at EK+, and qPCR showing increased mGluR7 expression with E2. The mGluR7 antagonist ADX71743 blocked ~90% of the response.

results.result: Kiss1ARH neurons send direct glutamatergic projections to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons, with enhanced glutamatergic input in E2-treated females as evidenced by reduced paired-pulse ratios.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 are supported by immunocytochemistry (Figure 6A) showing ChR2-mCherry labeled fibers in AVPV/PeN without cell bodies, optogenetic data (Figure 6C) showing TTX-sensitive, 4-AP-rescued responses, and PPR experiments (Figure 6D,E) showing reduced PPR in E2-treated animals.

results.result: Conditional deletion of Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons eliminates fast glutamatergic responses in Kiss1AVPV/PeN, POMC, and NPY/AgRP neurons following low-frequency optogenetic stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C85, C89-C91, C126 are supported by scRT-PCR (Figure 11A) confirming absence of Slc17a6 mRNA in KO neurons while Tac2 is present, and optogenetic experiments (Figure 12) showing complete absence of fast glutamatergic responses in all three target neuron populations from KO animals.

results.result: Deletion of Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons leads to conditioned place preference for sucrose and increased sucrose consumption in E2-treated KO female mice, with Het mice showing intermediate phenotype, while control E2-treated females show diminished motivation for sucrose.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C107-C114, C127 are supported by CPP behavioral data (Figure 16A,B) showing significant preference for sucrose-paired chamber and increased sucrose intake in KO mice, with Het mice showing intermediate effects. Statistical analyses with appropriate two-way ANOVA and post-hoc tests are reported. The gene-dosage effect is supported by qPCR showing ~35% Slc17a6 expression in Het mice.

results.result: High-frequency stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons in Slc17a6 KO mice evokes small residual currents in POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons, likely mediated by kisspeptin acting through Kiss1 receptors (GPR54) in POMC neurons and NPFFR1 in NPY/AgRP neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94, C95-C96, C100-C105 are supported by optogenetic data (Figure 12H-J) showing small residual currents in KO animals, scRT-PCR (Figures 13D, 14A) showing receptor expression, and pharmacology (Figures 13, 14) showing kisspeptin and RFRP-3 effects. However, C94 is speculative as selective peptide antagonists were not available to definitively prove kisspeptin mediation.

results.result: Deletion of Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons significantly reduces the slow EPSP amplitude in Kiss1ARH neurons from E2-treated but not oil-treated OVX females, suggesting glutamate contributes to the slow EPSP in E2-treated animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by optogenetic data (Figure 11) showing similar slow EPSP amplitudes in oil-treated control and KO mice, but significantly reduced slow EPSP in E2-treated KO versus control mice. The inference that glutamate contributes to the slow EPSP in E2-treated animals is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Deletion of Slc17a6 in Kiss1 neurons does not affect estrous cycle length or time to conception in female mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by estrous cycle monitoring and fertility measurements showing no significant differences between WT, Het, and KO groups (one-way ANOVA, p=0.68 for both measures). However, the authors note that cycle staging was not confirmed by hormone measurements, which is a limitation.

results.result: Tac2 mRNA is the most highly expressed transcript in Kiss1ARH neurons from OVX females, with expression levels 50-fold higher than Pdyn/Kiss1 and 6-fold higher than Slc17a6 in OVX females, and 18-fold higher than Pdyn in E2-treated females.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 1) with quantitative analysis using Tacr3 as calibrator. The fold-change calculations are based on CT values and appear methodologically sound. This establishes the relative abundance of different transcripts in Kiss1ARH neurons.

results.result: Slc32a1 (vGAT) mRNA was undetectable in Kiss1ARH neurons from both oil-treated and E2-treated OVX female mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 is supported by qPCR data showing Slc32a1 mRNA below the level of detectability (CT 36) in Kiss1ARH neurons. This indicates that GABA is not a primary neurotransmitter in these neurons, consistent with the functional data showing glutamate as the primary amino acid neurotransmitter.

results.result: Low-frequency optogenetic stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons produces equivalent fast glutamatergic input to both POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons in females, similar to findings in males.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by electrophysiological measurements showing no significant difference in evoked fast PSC amplitudes between POMC (25.8 ± 4.8 pA) and NPY/AgRP (33.3 ± 4.9 pA) neurons. The comparison to males is appropriately cited (Nestor et al., 2016).

results.result: There is a striking male/female difference in the effects of sex steroids on Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamate release in Kiss1ARH neurons, with testosterone inhibiting and estradiol enhancing glutamate signaling.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 is supported by the current findings showing E2 increases Slc17a6 expression and glutamate release in females, contrasted with cited findings (Nestor et al., 2016) showing testosterone decreases these parameters in males. This represents an important sex difference in neuroendocrine regulation.

results.result: Slc17a6 KO and Het mice did not show significant weight gain on standard chow over the study period, though Het mice showed statistically significant weight gain compared to controls. Slc17a6 mRNA in Het mice was ~35% of controls, and was undetectable in KO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C106, C115-C117 are supported by body weight measurements (Figure 16C) and qPCR data (Figure 16D). The lack of significant weight gain in KO mice on standard chow, despite increased motivation for palatable food, suggests the phenotype is specific to hedonic rather than homeostatic feeding.

results.result: Intact males, which have reduced Slc17a6 mRNA expression and glutamate release compared to E2-treated females, demonstrated motivation for sucrose based on CPP.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is supported by behavioral data (Figure 16—figure supplement 1) showing intact males developed CPP for sucrose, and is consistent with cited findings (Nestor et al., 2016) showing reduced Slc17a6 expression in intact versus castrated males. This provides additional context for the sex-specific regulation.

results.result: The E2-driven increase in Kiss1 neuronal excitability and glutamate neurotransmission may play a key role in governing motivational drive for palatable food and coordinating feeding and reproduction in females.
results.evaluation: Claims C11 and C128 are speculative conclusions that integrate multiple findings. While the data support that glutamate from Kiss1ARH neurons influences motivation for palatable food, the precise mechanisms and the coordination with reproduction require additional experiments. The claims appropriately use cautious language ('may play a key role').

results.result: Background claims about Kiss1 neuron populations, their regulation by E2, expression of neurotransmitters and receptors, and their roles in reproduction and feeding, based on cited literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C26, C97-C98, C121-C122 are background knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These establish the context for the current study and are generally well-established in the field. The citations appear appropriate and accurate.

results.result: High-frequency stimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons produces significantly different membrane potential changes in POMC versus NPY/AgRP neurons, with excitation of POMC and inhibition of NPY/AgRP neurons, presumably through glutamate spillover to extrasynaptic metabotropic receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 7F) showing statistically significant differences in membrane potential changes. The mechanism involving glutamate spillover is appropriately cited (Nietz et al., 2017; Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003) and is consistent with the high-frequency stimulation paradigm.

results.result: DHPG had no effect on NPY/AgRP neurons, DCG-IV had no effect on POMC neurons, and AMN082 had no effect on POMC neurons that responded to DHPG.
results.evaluation: Claims C73, C78, C82 are stated as negative results but the data are not shown. While these negative controls are important for establishing receptor specificity, the lack of presented data makes it difficult to fully evaluate these claims. The results are consistent with the scRT-PCR data showing differential receptor expression.

results.result: Summary claims integrating findings that E2 differentially regulates amino acid versus peptide neurotransmitters in Kiss1ARH neurons, increases neuronal excitability, and enables frequency-dependent glutamatergic and peptidergic neurotransmission to feeding-related neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C125 are summary statements that accurately integrate the experimental findings presented in the manuscript. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective data from molecular, electrophysiological, and behavioral experiments.
